title: The Ladder of Inference: Why Two People in the Same Meeting Walk Away With Different Realities
author: The Good Boss
summary: The Ladder of Inference is a mental model that describes how people unconsciously move from observable data to firm beliefs and decisive action through a rapid series of interpretive steps. Starting from raw events, we selectively notice certain data, assign cultural meanings to what we observe, make assumptions, draw conclusions, form beliefs, and act—all within seconds and often without awareness. For managers, this process is a recurring source of miscommunication and poor personnel decisions: a terse email, a delayed response, or a flat tone can trigger a full inference chain ending in a snap judgment about someone's commitment or attitude. The article explains each rung of the ladder in detail and shows how different people observing the same event can reach completely opposite interpretations based on the assumptions they bring. The Rung Check Technique provides managers a practical pause point for identifying which rung they are currently on and separating observable facts from the layers of interpretation they have added. With regular practice, leaders can reduce interpersonal conflict and make more accurate, fairer assessments of their team members.
points: The Ladder of Inference describes six unconscious steps from raw observable data to decisive action, explaining why two people in the same meeting can walk away with opposite conclusions
Managers are especially susceptible to incomplete inference chains that turn brief ambiguous signals—a terse reply, a delayed email—into definitive judgments about team members' attitudes
The Rung Check Technique helps leaders pause and identify which rung they are on, separating observable facts from the assumptions and interpretations layered on top of them
quotes: In this issue: The Email That Ruined my Afternoon The Ladder of Inference The Six Rungs How This Shows Up for Managers Putting the Ladder Into Practice The Rung Check Technique How This Plays Out in Real Teams Common Pitfalls (and How to Avoid Them) Final Thoughts The Email That Ruined my Afternoon A few years ago, I was putting together a proposal for a new project I felt strongly about.
It was genuinely excited about it and put in real effort into building the case: why it mattered and the data to back it up.
I made sure that I was thorough enough so there was nothing left to poke holes in.
Finally, that Wednesday afternoon, after reviewing it a few times, I attached the deck to an email to my manager, and hit send, full of anticipation.
My manager’s reply came back within the hour: “Let’s discuss.” That was it.
No “great idea,” no “let’s talk logistics,” not even a question mark.
I spent the rest of that afternoon dismantling my own proposal in my head.
Maybe this was the polite version of “no.” I then started rehearsing how I’d defend it when I do get to ‘discuss’ it with him.
